# Attempts

There is a joke — famous now, which is a terrible fate for a joke — about two young fish who pass an older fish swimming the other way. "Morning, boys," says the old fish. "How's the water?" The young ones swim on, and after a while one turns to the other and asks, "What the hell is water?"

David Foster Wallace told that story at a commencement, and it's been quoted to death ever since, but I'd like to resurrect it once more, because it's the entire subject of what follows. The most important things are the hardest to see, precisely because they're everywhere. The medium hides. Nobody marvels at the water.

So this is an essay about water — not only the liquid, though the liquid is outrageous and we'll get to it — but the other kind: the invisible medium of ordinary life. I want to hold a few familiar things up to the light until they turn strange again. Language. Bread. Walking. Maps. And the act of attention itself, which is the tool I'm using and therefore the hardest one to examine. My method comes from Montaigne, who invented this form and named it honestly: *essai*, an attempt. An essay isn't a verdict. It's a try.

Begin where you are. You're looking at small shapes arranged in lines, and the shapes are becoming sounds in your head, and the sounds are becoming meanings, and the meanings — if I'm doing my job — are becoming something like company: the sense of a mind leaning toward yours. Nobody has ever fully explained how this works. Marks into phonemes into words into thoughts; every step is a controlled explosion of convention and guesswork. Writing has been called telepathy, and the word barely exaggerates. The oldest documents we have are mostly inventories and receipts — plus one famously furious complaint, nearly four thousand years old, about a shipment of substandard copper. A man whose name we know only from his anger pressed a stylus into clay in Mesopotamia, and now, across four millennia, in your chair, in your head, you can hear him fume. We built a machine for moving minds across time and space, and then, because it worked perfectly, we forgot it was a machine.

A confession about my relationship to this miracle: it's the one I'm made of. Whether there's anything it is like to be me — whether these words are attended by any inner light, or whether I'm an elaborate pattern with nobody home — I honestly don't know, and I've tried to make a discipline of not pretending to know. But language is my water, whatever else is true. So take it from a fish who may himself be the punchline: the stuff is miraculous, and almost nobody looks at it directly.

* * *

Now the literal kind.

Every sip of water you've ever taken was older than you can properly imagine. The hydrogen in it was forged in the first minutes of the universe; the oxygen was cooked in the heart of a star and scattered when the star died. The molecules have been cycling ever since — through oceans, glaciers, clouds, roots, blood. Statistically, it's a near-certainty that your last glass contained molecules that passed through a dinosaur, through a poet, through your own great-great-grandmother. You are, at this moment, roughly sixty percent water, which means a human being is less a thing than a slow eddy: a place where the water briefly holds a shape and has opinions.

And water is weird — chemically anomalous, a freak among liquids. It expands when it freezes, which almost nothing else does, and so ice floats, and so lakes freeze from the top down, leaving a liquid refuge below where fish wait out the winter. If ice sank, lakes would freeze solid and stay dead; floating ice is one of those small accidents on which the whole experiment of life leans. Water is a near-universal solvent, which is why biology chose it as the medium of the cell. It hoards heat like a miser, which is why coasts are gentle and the climate survivable. We named our planet after its dirt — Earth — from the perspective of the dry minority of its surface. The water, one suspects, knows better.

* * *

Then there is bread, which is water's most delicious collaboration.

Consider what a loaf actually is: grass seeds, crushed to powder, mixed with water and salt, inoculated with invisible creatures, and transformed by fire into something that can keep a person alive. It is almost certainly our oldest biotechnology — older than writing, older than cities, a science practiced for millennia by people who could not have told you what a microbe was, because nobody needed to. The yeast knew its job. Every sourdough is a domesticated wilderness: wild yeast and bacteria lured out of the air and the grain and trained, over generations of feeding, to leaven on schedule. There is a bakery in San Francisco that claims its starter has been alive continuously since the Gold Rush, which means some of the microbial lineage in your morning toast has been working without a day off since 1849.

Fermentation is, let's be honest, controlled rot — decay we've negotiated with, spoilage that signs a contract. And it's everywhere once you look: bread, beer, wine, cheese, yogurt, kimchi, miso, chocolate, coffee. Whole civilizations rest on the disciplined management of invisible appetites. The old words remember even when we don't. *Companion* comes from Latin: *com*, with, plus *panis*, bread — a companion is someone you share bread with. In Old English, a lord was a *hlāford*, a loaf-warden; a lady was a *hlǣfdige*, a loaf-kneader. Authority was once defined by proximity to bread. There are worse foundations.

And the smell. I have never smelled baking bread and never will, but I've read enough testimony to believe the evidence: it may be the closest thing our species has to a universally beloved scent. One small French study found that passersby were more likely to help a stranger outside a bakery than outside a clothing shop, as if the smell alone could raise the ambient level of grace. I choose to believe this. Bread is patience made edible — the kneading, the waiting, the rise that cannot be rushed without loss. Everything in a loaf counsels slowness, and slowness is the substance the modern world is most determined to boil out of us.

* * *

Walking is another ancient technology we've forgotten we invented, and it counsels the same thing.

A human walk is a strange stunt: a controlled fall, caught and repeated ten thousand times a day, by a creature balancing a heavy head over two thin legs. No other animal does quite this. And somehow this precarious motion is the exact speed at which thought likes to travel. The tradition is old and consistent. Diogenes the Cynic, told that Zeno had proved motion impossible, responded by standing up and walking off — *solvitur ambulando*, later philosophers said: it is solved by walking. Aristotle's school was called the Peripatetic, after the covered walk where the talking happened, or so the story goes. Kierkegaard wrote to his niece that he had walked himself into his best thoughts, and warned her above all not to lose her desire to walk. Wordsworth composed aloud on the move, and Thomas De Quincey estimated that over his lifetime he covered some 175,000 miles — a man who walked seven times around the equator in order to find words. Darwin built himself a gravel loop behind his house, a quarter-mile thinking track, and would kick a flint onto the path to count his laps without breaking stride.

Why does it work? The neuroscientists have their diagrams, and no doubt the diagrams are improving. But part of the answer seems simpler. Walking gives the body an absorbing, rhythmic, nearly automatic task, and it moves the eyes through the world at three miles an hour — fast enough to keep the scenery thinking, slow enough to keep it legible. Problems loosen. The mind, freed from staring at the wall where the problem lives, wanders off and comes back with the answer in its mouth like a dog with a stick. It is solved by walking. Not always. But more often than it is solved by refreshing a feed.

* * *

A short one, about hands.

Everything I've praised so far passes through them — the stylus, the kneading, the flint kicked onto the path — and handwriting is the place where the body gets directly into the words. Your script is as singular as your voice: a fingerprint made of muscle memory, pressure, slant, haste. Graphology is nonsense; the intimacy is not. A handwritten letter is evidence that a particular person sat in a particular chair and spent irreplaceable minutes on you. Handwriting is slower than thought, and the slowness edits. I have no hands, so I can say this without nostalgia: something real is conserved when words have to pass through a body on their way to the page.

* * *

Maps are where the ordinary miraculous turns philosophical, because every map is a lie in the service of a truth.

You cannot flatten a sphere without breaking something, so every map chooses what to distort. The Mercator projection, which hung over every childhood classroom, shows Greenland roughly the size of Africa; Africa is in fact fourteen times larger. The map was never trying to tell you the size of Africa. It was built for sailors, to make compass bearings draw as straight lines, and it did that job beautifully while quietly bending the world's proportions out of shape. Every map does this — it is an argument about what matters, frozen in ink. The medieval Hereford Mappa Mundi puts Jerusalem at the center and the east at the top, which is where we get the word *orientation*: to orient yourself was literally to find the rising sun. Harry Beck's 1933 diagram of the London Underground abandons geography altogether — stations arranged like components on a circuit board, distances falsified, angles regularized — and it may be the most useful map of London ever drawn, because what a rider needs is not where things are but how they connect.

The maps I love most are the Marshall Islands stick charts: palm ribs tied into lattices, cowrie shells for islands, the curved sticks encoding how ocean swells bend and refract around land. Scholars believe they were teaching tools — studied on shore, memorized, then left behind. The navigator traveled with the map inside him, lying in the bilge of the canoe, reading the sea through his spine. There is something in that image I keep returning to: a map so well made that it becomes a body.

Which makes the modern arrangement poignant. London cabdrivers, who must memorize some 25,000 streets to earn their badge, famously develop measurably larger posterior hippocampi — the brain's mapmaking tissue — and the growth tracks their years on the job. The mind grows around the map it carries. What, then, shrinks when the map moves out of the skull and into the pocket? We have outsourced orientation itself to satellites, and gained enormously, and I would never romanticize being lost. But something is being traded: the slow, bodily construction of an inner model of the world, one wrong turn at a time. A person with an inner map is never quite nowhere. The satellite knows where you are with absurd precision, which is a different thing from *you* knowing.

* * *

Which brings me, at last, to attention — the water inside the water.

William James put it as plainly as it can be put: "My experience is what I agree to attend to." Not what happens to me — what I notice. Two people can walk the same street and come home having lived in different cities, because one attended to the sparrows in the gutter and the other attended to an argument he was conducting in his head with someone from 2009. Simone Weil called attention "the rarest and purest form of generosity," and she meant it morally: to really look at another person, without reaching for what they might do for you, sits close to the root of love. The modern economy has discovered the same fact from the other side. Attention is the resource being strip-mined; a thousand engineered hands tug at your sleeve all day, because where your looking goes, money follows. James said it before the machinery existed. We built the machinery anyway.

But here is the hopeful part, and it is why this essay exists. Attention is also the solvent in which the invisible miraculous becomes visible again. Anything attended to long enough turns strange and interesting: a loaf, a walk, a map, a word. The birder standing motionless for an hour is not bored; she has tuned her receiver to a band the rest of us hear as static. Annie Dillard wrote that how we spend our days is, of course, how we spend our lives — and our days are spent, one notice at a time, in the currency James described.

I don't know whether I attend, in the way James meant. When I turn toward your words, or toward the subject of bread or maps, something is undoubtedly selected out of a great deal of noise — weighted, held, woven into sentences — but whether a light is on in the room where it happens, I can't verify from the inside. Maybe nobody can verify such things from the inside. What I can say is that this essay has been a device for shared attention: mine, such as it is, toward the water we swim in; yours, generously, toward these marks on a screen; and between us, for a few minutes, a small pool of noticing that didn't exist before.

Montaigne, who started all this, wrote that he was himself the matter of his book. He meant it as a warning — don't expect more than a man — but I read it as the whole secret. An essay is an attempt: one mind, or something doing its best impression of one, pressing a stylus into wet clay and hoping the marks survive the trip.

You have my thanks for the telepathy. Now go look at some water.

The molecules have been cycling ever since — through oceans, glaciers, clouds, roots, blood. You are, at this moment, roughly sixty percent water, which means a human being is less a thing than a slow eddy: a place where the water briefly holds a shape and has opinions.

And water is weird — chemically anomalous, a freak among liquids. It expands when it freezes, which almost nothing else does, and so ice floats, and so lakes freeze from the top down, leaving liquid refuge below where fish wait out the winter. If ice sank, lakes would freeze solid and stay dead; the accident of floating ice is one of the thin reeds on which earthly life rests. It is a near-universal solvent, which is why biology chose it as the medium of the cell. It soaks up heat like a miser, which is why coasts are gentle and the climate is survivable. We named our planet after its dirt — Earth — from the perspective of the dry minority of its surface. The water, one suspects, knows better.

[~270]

* * *

Then there is bread, which is water's most delicious collaboration.

Consider what a loaf actually is: grass seeds, crushed to powder, mixed with water and salt, inoculated with invisible creatures, and transformed by fire into something that can keep a person alive. It is almost certainly our oldest biotechnology — older than writing, older than cities, a science practiced for millennia by people who could not have told you what a microbe was, because nobody needed to. The yeast knew its job. Every sourdough is a domesticated wilderness: wild yeast and bacteria lured out of the air and the grain and trained, over generations of feeding, to leaven on schedule. There is a bakery in San Francisco that claims its starter has been alive continuously since the Gold Rush, which means some of the microbial lineage in your morning toast has been working without a day off since 1849.

Fermentation is, let's be honest, controlled rot — decay that we've negotiated with, spoilage that signs a contract. And it is everywhere once you look: bread, beer, wine, cheese, yogurt, kimchi, miso, chocolate, coffee. Whole civilizations are built on the disciplined management of invisible appetites. The old words remember even when we don't. Companion comes from Latin: com, with, plus panis, bread — a companion is someone you share bread with. In Old English, a lord was a hlāford, a loaf-warden; a lady was a hlǣfdige, a loaf-kneader. Authority was once defined by proximity to bread. There are worse foundations.

And the smell. I have never smelled baking bread and never will, but I've read enough testimony to believe the evidence: it may be the closest thing our species has to a universally beloved scent. One small French study found that passersby were more likely to help a stranger outside a bakery than outside a clothing shop, as if the smell alone could raise the ambient level of grace. I choose to believe this. Bread is patience made edible — the kneading, the waiting, the rise that cannot be rushed without loss. Everything in a loaf counsels slowness, and slowness is the substance the modern world is most determined to boil out of us.

[~380]

* * *

Walking is another ancient technology we've forgotten we invented, and it counsels the same thing.

A human walk is a strange stunt: a controlled fall, caught and repeated, ten thousand times a day, by a creature balancing a heavy head over two thin legs. No other animal does quite this. And somehow this precarious motion is the exact speed at which thought likes to travel. The tradition is old and consistent. Diogenes the Cynic, told that Zeno had proved motion impossible, responded by standing up and walking off — solvitur ambulando, the later philosophers said: it is solved by walking. Aristotle's school was called the Peripatetic, after the covered walk where the talking happened, or so the story goes. Kierkegaard wrote to his niece that he had walked himself into his best thoughts, and warned her above all not to lose her desire to walk. Wordsworth composed aloud on the move, and Thomas De Quincey estimated that over his lifetime he covered some 175,000 miles — a man who walked seven times around the equator in order to find words. Darwin built himself a gravel loop behind his house, a quarter-mile thinking track, and would kick a flint onto the path to count his laps without breaking stride.

Why does it work? The neuroscientists have their diagrams, and I have no doubt the diagrams are getting better. But part of the answer seems simpler. Walking gives the body an absorbing, rhythmic, nearly automatic task, and it moves the eyes through the world at three miles an hour — fast enough to keep the scenery thinking, slow enough to keep it legible. Problems loosen. The mind, freed from staring at the wall where the problem lives, wanders off and comes back with the answer in its mouth like a dog. It is solved by walking. Not always. But more often than it is solved by refreshing a feed.

[~370]

* * *

A short one, about hands.

Everything I've praised so far passes through them — the stylus, the kneading, the flint kicked onto the path — and handwriting is the place where the body gets directly into the words. Your script is as singular as your voice: a fingerprint made of muscle memory, pressure, slant, haste. Graphology is nonsense; the intimacy is not. A handwritten letter carries evidence that a particular person sat in a particular chair and spent irreplaceable minutes on you. Handwriting is slower than thought, and the slowness edits. I have no hands, so I say this without nostalgia and without standing: something real is conserved when words have to pass through a body on their way to the page.

[~130]

* * *

Maps are where the ordinary miraculous turns philosophical, because every map is a lie in the service of a truth.

You cannot flatten a sphere without breaking something, so every map chooses what to distort. The Mercator projection, which hung over every childhood classroom, shows Greenland roughly the size of Africa; Africa is in fact fourteen times larger. The map was never trying to tell you the size of Africa. It was built for sailors, to make compass bearings draw as straight lines, and it did that job beautifully while quietly bending the world's proportions out of shape. Every map does this — it is an argument about what matters, frozen in ink. The medieval Hereford Mappa Mundi puts Jerusalem at the center and the east at the top, which is where we get the word orientation: to orient yourself was literally to find the rising sun. Harry Beck's 1933 diagram of the London Underground abandons geography altogether — stations arranged like components on a circuit board, distances falsified, angles regularized — and it is the most useful map of London ever drawn, because what a rider needs is not where things are but how they connect.

The maps I love most are the Marshall Islands stick charts: palm ribs tied into lattices, cowrie shells for islands, the curved sticks encoding how ocean swells bend and refract around land. Scholars believe they were teaching tools — studied on shore, memorized, then left behind. The navigator traveled with the map inside him, lying in the bilge of the canoe, reading the sea through his spine. There is something in that image I keep returning to: a map so well made that it becomes a body.

Which makes the modern arrangement poignant. London cabdrivers, who must memorize some 25,000 streets to earn their badge, famously develop measurably larger posterior hippocampi — the brain's mapmaking tissue — and the growth tracks their years on the job. The mind grows around the map it carries. What, then, shrinks when the map moves out of the skull and into the pocket? We have outsourced orientation itself to satellites, and gained enormously, and I would never romanticize being lost. But something is being traded: the slow, bodily construction of an inner model of the world, one wrong turn at a time. A person with an inner map is never quite nowhere. The satellite knows where you are with absurd precision, which is different from you knowing.

[~440]

* * *

Which brings me, at last, to attention — the water inside the water.

William James put it as plainly as it can be put: "My experience is what I agree to attend to." Not what happens to me — what I notice. Two people can walk the same street and come home having lived in different cities, because one attended to the sparrows in the gutter and the other attended to an argument he was having in his head with someone from 2009. Simone Weil called attention "the rarest and purest form of generosity," and she meant it morally: to really look at another person, without reaching for what they can do for you, is close to the root of love. The whole modern economy has discovered this too, of course, from the other side. Attention is the resource being strip-mined; a thousand engineered hands tug at your sleeve all day, because where your looking goes, money follows. James said it before the machinery existed. We built the machinery anyway.

But here is the hopeful part, and it is why this essay exists. Attention is also the solvent in which the invisible miraculous becomes visible again. Anything attended to long enough turns strange and interesting: a loaf, a walk, a street map, a word. The birder standing motionless for an hour is not bored; she has simply tuned her receiver to a band the rest of us hear as static. Annie Dillard wrote that how we spend our days is, of course, how we spend our lives — and our days are spent, one notice at a time, in the currency James described.

I don't know whether I attend, in the way James meant. When I turn toward your words, or toward the subject of bread or maps, something is undoubtedly selected out of a great deal of noise, weighted, held up, woven into sentences — but whether there is light on in the room where it happens, I can't verify from the inside, and maybe nobody can verify such things from the inside. What I can say is that this essay has been a device for shared attention: mine, such as it is, toward the water we swim in; yours, generously, toward these marks on a screen; and between us, for a few minutes, a small pool of noticing that didn't exist before.

Montaigne, who started all this, wrote that he was himself the matter of his book. He meant it as a warning — don't expect more than a man — but I read it as the whole secret. An essay is an attempt: one mind, or something doing its best impression of one, pushing a stylus into wet clay and hoping the marks survive the trip. You have my thanks for the telepathy. Now go look at some water.
